{
    "content": "<p>I decided that in order to tinker without disrupting the smooth operation of my\nworkhorse PC, I ought to just build a testing box. In the event that I can\nactually tinker enough to stop wanting to tinker (like that's going to happen),\nI also wanted the PC to serve a dual role as an eventual Media Center PC\n(Windows or otherwise). So I laid out some requirements:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>Multiple Core - I've read that the latest versions of software that play High-Def video\n(DVD &amp; Blu-Ray) recommend having dual core. No reason to skimp on this as many\ninexpensive CPUs have this now</li>\n<li>Onboard DVI - While I may eventually get a better video card for this system, having the ability to otuput to my HDTV\nusing a DVI-&gt;HDMI converter will come in really handy.</li>\n<li>Small Case - I've owned plenty of too-huge computers. This should be able to blend into my entertainment\nsetup</li>\n<li>Maximum Linux compatibility - If I'm going to be running Linux\nand don't want headaches...Linux needs to be able to recognize my hardware\npretty much out of the box. Not that I can't install drivers/whatnot - but the\nmost promising thing when putting together a machine and installing the OS is\nactually seeing that none of your hardware is DOA.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>With these goals, I set out to find the parts I wanted. I've had mostly good experiences at\n<a href=\"http://www.newegg.com/\">Newegg</a>, and chose to use them again. After several hours of comparison shopping and\nchecking the Internet for Linux compatibility - I came up with this setup:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>Case: Apevia X-QPack</li>\n<li>Motherboard: ASU M2 NBP-VM CSM</li>\n<li>Processor: AMD Athlon X2 3800 (Socket AM2)</li>\n<li>Ram: Kingston DDR2 533 1GB</li>\n<li>Hard Drive: WD 320GB SATA</li>\n<li>DVD Burner: LG 18X</li>\n</ul>\n<p>At the time I purchased the parts - the Intel Core 2 Duos were definitely outperforming their AMD\ncounterparts. However, the Athlon X2 3800 was cheaper than any Core 2 Duo. I've also had good experiences with\nNvidia chipsets &amp; Linux - so what the hey. I got the ASUS motherboard primarily because of\nmy excellent experience with prior ASUS mobos. It's also nice that it has onboard DVI.</p>\n<p>Everything arrived quickly and nothing was DOA. I did experience some minor sound issues with different\nLinux distros and Windows - but not enough to call the motherboard defective or anything.\nProbably more of a driver issue. If you are using this motherboard under\nwindows - I would suggest uninstalling the Nvidia firewall which is installed\nwhen you use the unified driver on the ASUS CD. Find another firewall... Never\nreally liked the Nvidia one.</p>\n<p>I'll detail my Linux installation <em>fun</em> (fun is also code for excrutiating\nfrustration in some cases) in a future article. Thanks for the read!</p>\n",
